venues.d: The Nizam's own palace on a hilltop above the old city — one of the greatest hotels in India, and it feels it.

venues.n: ITC Kohenur, a Luxury Collection Hotel
venues.d: A Luxury Collection tower named for the Koh-i-Noor, overlooking the lake in the new-city business heart.
Contemporary Hyatt luxury in the city's most distinguished neighbourhood — calm, design-led, quietly grand.
The Taj's grande-dame in Banjara Hills — thirteen acres of green in the heart of the old-money city.
The Oberoi group's polished HITEC City house — understated, faultlessly run, in the tech heart.
Fifteen garden acres beside India's largest convention centre — the natural base for a large gathering.
Royal Hyderabadi cooking on the palace terrace, the Nizam's city glittering below — the grandest table in Hyderabad.
Hyderabad's most-loved vegetarian house — South Indian tiffin and thalis done with real pride.
India's most talked-about chocolate — bean-to-bar from Indian cacao, in a café that has put Hyderabad on the national food map.
The name Hyderabad gave the world for biryani — a legend since 1953, and still the first plate visitors are told to eat.
The biryani (and Ramzan haleem) Hyderabadis choose to impress a visitor — heavier on ghee, closer to the old Nizami style.
The Old City institution by the Charminar — biryani, kebabs and Ramzan haleem in the thick of old Hyderabad.
A decades-old single-location legend — for many locals, simply the best mutton biryani in the city.
Hyderabad's home-grown dining group since 1976 — from the cavernous Gufaa to grand banquet halls, a city institution.

The 1591 four-minaret gateway is the soul of the old city, its granite arches rising over the chaos of the bazaars around it. Climb the narrow spiral stair at golden hour, then let a private guide thread you through the lanes below.

The lane radiating from the Charminar is a river of lacquer bangles, pearls and bridal finery, unchanged in trade for four centuries. A trusted dealer will bring the good pearls out from the back, away from the crush.

One of India's largest and oldest mosques, its central arches raised from bricks said to be brought from Mecca, holding ten thousand worshippers beside the Charminar. Dress modestly; the courtyard is best in the quiet before Friday prayers.

The Qutb Shahi citadel climbs a granite hill in concentric ramparts, and its famous acoustics carry a hand-clap at the entrance clear to the pavilion on top. A dawn climb before the heat, with a guide who knows the water system and the secret passages, is the way to do it.

After dark the ramparts light in sequence while a narrated history of the fort and the Koh-i-Noor plays across the stone, English on set evenings. Book the English show ahead and carry a wrap; the hilltop cools fast.

The necropolis of the sultans, thirty domed tombs and a mortuary bath in a garden below the fort, has been meticulously restored over the past decade and reopened as a heritage park. It is quieter and more moving than the fort; go with someone who can read the calligraphy.

The Nizams' ceremonial seat, four palaces around courtyards and a Belgian-crystal Durbar Hall, with the vintage-car collection and a 1930s Rolls in the forecourt. It is the clearest window onto Asaf Jahi grandeur; take the guided route to catch the details.

venues.n: Taj Falaknuma Palace — high tea and heritage walk
venues.d: The Nizam's cloud-palace, 2,000 feet above the city, is now a Taj hotel, and the afternoon heritage walk with an art historian ends in high tea served on the Jade Terrace or in the Gol Bungalow. This is the single most Nizami afternoon in Hyderabad; the day tour is booked in advance and usually runs weekends.

venues.n: A night at Taj Falaknuma Palace
venues.d: To actually stay is to dine at the world's longest banquet table, be received at the porte-cochere with rose petals, and walk the Jade Room and library after the day guests have gone. For a multi-generational trip it is the anchor experience; suites go quickly.

The world's largest one-man collection, some 43,000 objects amassed by Salar Jung III, from the Veiled Rebecca marble to a musical clock that draws a crowd on the hour. Half a day with a curator-led guide barely scratches it; closed Fridays.

The sixth Nizam's 176-foot Burmese-teak walk-in wardrobe with its hand-cranked lift, and the silver-jubilee gifts of the last Nizam, fill the old family palace. It is intimate and eccentric where Chowmahalla is grand; a short, rewarding stop.

A hidden 18th-century necropolis of the Nizams' nobility, its lime-stucco and pierced marble jaali screens so fine they draw comparison to the Alhambra, now beautifully restored. Few tourists find it; go with a guide who can point out the geometry.

A Qutb Shahi pleasure pavilion of arched bays set on a rise near Golconda, tied to the legend of the courtesan whose song carried to the fort. Restored as a cultural venue, it is a serene stop and a fine sunset perch.

venues.n: Hussain Sagar and the Buddha statue
venues.d: The heart-shaped lake dug in 1563 holds a single 58-foot monolithic Buddha on a mid-water rock, reached by a short boat ride. A dusk cruise from Lumbini Park, city lights coming up around the water, is the classic pause.

The lamp-lit promenade curving along the lake takes its name from the way it strings the shore like a necklace of lights. It is where the city walks in the evening; good for a slow stroll or a private car cruise before dinner.

A white-marble Vishnu temple on a granite hill, carved in Rajasthani and Dravidian styles, glowing at dusk above the lake. The climb rewards you with the best free panorama of the twin cities; leave footwear and cameras at the base.

venues.n: B. M. Birla Science Museum and Planetarium
venues.d: Below the temple, the planetarium's dome-projected sky shows and the science galleries with a dinosaur skeleton are a genuine hit with children. A good hour for a multi-generational group needing a change of pace from monuments.

An arts-and-crafts village where weavers, bidri-workers and dyers sell direct, with a rolling rural bazaar and folk performances at the amphitheatre. It is the easiest place to meet artisans and buy well without haggling in the old-city crush.

venues.n: Durgam Cheruvu and the cable bridge
venues.d: A rock-fringed lake once hidden inside the tech corridor, now crossed by a floodlit extradosed cable bridge that changes colour at night. It is the modern face of the city; walk the lakeside boardwalk after dark for the light show on the water.

A pocket of Deccan scrub forest in the smartest part of town, its shaded loop a favourite morning walk for peacocks, wildflowers and the city's power-walkers. A calm green start to a day; go at opening for the birds.

One of India's larger zoos, with a lion-and-tiger safari drive-through and a nocturnal-animals house, set in green near the old city. An easy multi-generational morning; the safari bus is the draw for children.

The dum biryani — rice and meat sealed and slow-cooked, served with mirchi-ka-salan and dahi chutney — is the city's edible crown, and every family swears by a different house. A private food guide can run a tasting across the legends, with the vegetable and kachche-gosht versions side by side.

venues.n: The Irani café ritual — Irani chai and Osmania biscuits
venues.d: The Persian-origin cafés of Hyderabad pour strong sweet Irani chai alongside the crumbly, faintly savoury Osmania biscuit — a century-old morning rite. Ten minutes at a marble-topped table tells you more about the city than an hour in a museum.

During Ramzan the lanes fill with the slow-pounded wheat-and-meat haleem, a Hyderabadi speciality with its own protected geographical status, cooked overnight in vast cauldrons. If your trip lands in the holy month, an evening haleem crawl is unmissable.

Amid the famous meat there is a deep vegetarian table too — bagara baingan, the tamarind-and-lentil pappu, and the fiery banana-leaf Andhra meals of the tech-city restaurants. Worth booking for travellers who don't eat meat but still want the regional flavour.

Hyderabad has been India's pearl-drilling and trading capital for centuries, and the old houses around the Charminar still sort, drill and string by hand. Buy from an established, certified house; a knowledgeable guide keeps you clear of the imitations.

Bidriware — black zinc alloy inlaid with silver in floral Persian motifs — is a Deccan art with its own GI tag, and Hyderabad is a prime place to buy the finest pieces. A vase or a paandan makes the most characterful souvenir of the region.

The centuries-old flea market spreads on Sundays into a maze of colonial-era brass, old cameras, vinyl and Nizam-era curios. A treasure hunt for collectors; go early with a local who can spot the real from the reproduced.

A restored 1930s Osmanian-Gothic market building, its clock tower now floodlit, famous for its old-school fruit ice-creams and the buzz of the surrounding lanes. A characterful evening stop between the old and new cities.

A guided morning on foot through the old-city lanes ties the palace, the mosque, the Charminar and the bazaars into a single narrative of the Qutb Shahi and Asaf Jahi city. The best single way to grasp how the old Hyderabad fits together; go early to beat the heat.

Telangana's flagship public art museum holds a broad collection of modern and contemporary Indian work in a purpose-built gallery near the tech corridor. A cool, uncrowded hour for those who want art beyond the antiquities.

A gloriously eccentric private collection of hand-built working cars shaped like a shoe, a cricket bat, a burger and more — the largest such museum of its kind. Odd, joyful and a sure hit with children.

venues.n: Lumbini Park and the lake laser show
venues.d: The lakeside park is the jetty for the Buddha-statue boats and stages an evening musical laser-fountain show on the water. A gentle sunset add-on to a lake cruise, easy with young family.

A rare Moorish-revival mosque with octagonal spires modelled on Andalusian Spain, built by a Paigah noble and unlike anything else in India. A quiet architectural curiosity a short drive from the airport road.

venues.n: Toli Masjid and the Qutb Shahi road to Golconda
venues.d: A 1671 mosque of exquisite stucco arches on the historic road between the city and Golconda, often missed on the standard circuit. For those who have done the headline monuments and want the connoisseur's stop.

The Guinness-certified largest film studio complex in the world, 2,000 acres of permanent sets, gardens and shows that double as a theme park. A full day, best with a premium guided package and a golf-cart tour; superb for multi-generational groups.

A single colossal egg-shaped granite monolith crowned by a Kakatiya-era fort, with a stiff stepped climb to sweeping Deccan views. Close enough for a half-day; now also a spot for rock-climbing and rappelling.

venues.n: Gol Bungalow / palace terraces, Taj Falaknuma Palace
venues.d: A drink on the Nizam's own palace terrace, the city's lights spread below — the grandest evening in Hyderabad.

venues.n: The Living Room, Park Hyatt Hyderabad
venues.d: A serene, design-led lounge in the city's best-run luxury hotel — considered cocktails, quiet and adult.
A long-standing Banjara Hills hotel bar — clubby, discreet, part of the city's social furniture for decades.
